arxiv:2611.09792.text: Knowing When to Intervene: Causal Evaluation of AI Agents. From Ayush Sawarni and colleagues. Benchmarks cannot show whether checking or steering an AI agent during a task will improve its final outcome. This work introduces a framework that uses a relatively small set of agent trajectories with randomized interventions to estimate how interventions affect outcomes in different contexts. Applied to three agent benchmarks, it finds that intervention effects vary substantially across actions and states. The estimates can also help practitioners prioritize which agent actions to audit.

arxiv:2611.09790.text: Box-Cox Transformations of Correlation Matrices. From Ilya Archakov and colleagues. Correlation matrices are awkward to parametrize because their entries must obey joint constraints. This work studies a family of Box-Cox transformations, including raw correlations and the Fisher transformation, and proves that each can be uniquely inverted. Only transformations with a power of zero or less cover all possible real-valued coordinates; among them, the Fisher transformation has the best conditioning bound. For Gaussian data, it also preserves identity covariance to first order in correlations, while a different power makes the leading third cumulant vanish at independence.

arxiv:2611.09778.text: Quasipolynomial-Time Planning for Decodable POMDPs. From Oliver Dobson and colleagues. Planning in partially observable Markov decision processes is computationally hard, so researchers seek conditions that make it easier. This work gives quasipolynomial-time algorithms for approximate planning when observations allow the hidden state to be decoded with a fixed level of accuracy. This decodability condition is weaker than existing observability conditions, yet its optimal strength can be computed in polynomial time. The result offers an easier-to-check condition that unifies earlier approaches.

arxiv:2611.09771.text: A Cross-Domain TARA-to-NAC Rule Mapping Methodology: From Automotive OEM Networks to Energy Storage Systems. From Krishna Teja Medam and colleagues. Turning cybersecurity risk goals into enforceable network rules is not clearly covered by existing methods, and compliance standards are often handled separately. A six-step approach links each goal to a network access rule, a named enforcement point, and the threat record behind it, while keeping shared standards fixed and swapping in sector-specific rules. In a desk-based automotive example, it produced 23 rules covering 11 of 13 goals; an energy storage example produced six rules. The approach offers a reusable pattern, but has not yet been tested in practice.

arxiv:2611.09619.text: Beyond Feasibility: Efficient and Robust On-Device Localization with UWB Concurrent Transmissions. From Enrico Soprana and colleagues. Concurrent ultra-wideband transmissions can speed up location updates and save energy, but earlier systems could not run directly on small tags or handle interference from other devices. This work redesigns the methods to run efficiently on resource-limited processors while preserving accuracy, and uses newer wireless features to resist interference and choose anchors dynamically. Tests in two real-world settings show that the complete system can locate itself on the tag, with up to forty-four percent lower runtime and eighty-five percent better energy efficiency than traditional methods.

arxiv:2611.09612.text: Kernel-Based Learning of Analytic Operators and Parametric PDEs. From Giovanni S. Alberti and colleagues. Learning an operator from a limited number of examples raises a key question: how should the kernel match the operator's smoothness? This work shows how analytic operators can be represented in kernel spaces and gives high-probability error guarantees for finite samples. With suitable analytic kernels, errors fall at an exponential rate in a fractional power of the sample count, while Sobolev-type kernels give polynomial rates. For a parametric elliptic equation, the analysis separates sampling error from finite-element error and guides how to choose the mesh size as the data set grows.

arxiv:2611.09579.text: Locally Adaptive Conformal Prediction for Polynomial Chaos Expansions. From Dimitrios Loukrezis and colleagues. Prediction intervals for polynomial chaos models can miss local changes in uncertainty, especially when noise varies across the input space. This work develops an adaptive jackknife-plus method that adjusts interval widths using an auxiliary model trained on leave-one-out errors. For fixed-basis models, it preserves the coverage guarantee and needs only one model fit; a faster shortcut for sparse models gives up that guarantee. Tests show target coverage with more efficient intervals, especially in regions of high uncertainty.

arxiv:2611.09141.text: Circuit Theory-Informed AI for Condition Monitoring in Power Electronics. From Yubo Song and colleagues. Condition monitoring in power electronics often relies on data-heavy artificial intelligence, while systems also have electrical behavior that can guide how data is read. This work presents a data-light approach that uses only three-phase alternating current measurements. It converts the current signals into voltage patterns in simple resistor-capacitor circuits, then uses spiking neural networks to estimate device parameters. Case studies validate the approach, and the work also discusses its limits and possible improvements.

arxiv:2611.09140.text: SPDMX: Large-Scale Open Stem Audio From Symbolic Music. From Phillip Long and colleagues. Copyright limits access to music audio, while many research tasks need separate instrument tracks rather than a finished mix. SPDMX turns public-domain music scores into an openly licensed collection of audio stems, with matching scores and an open rendering process. It contains more than five thousand song-hours, including over two thousand seven hundred hours with multiple tracks. This resource supports research on separating music sources, generating audio from scores, and linking musical notation with sound.

arxiv:2611.09060.text: Fair Selection of Generalized Nash Equilibria: A Comparability Perspective. From Sophie Hall and colleagues. Shared constraints can leave a game with many possible equilibria, and choosing one determines how agents share the cost of a scarce resource. This work examines those choices through comparability, a social choice idea about how people's costs can be compared. It shows that the usual variational equilibrium assumes a strong form of comparison by treating costs as measured in common units. The authors introduce a fair equilibrium that optimizes a fairness measure suited to the chosen comparison, and provide ways to compute it for several game types.

arxiv:2611.08936.text: Ordered Policy Optimization. From Dongkyu Derek Cho and colleagues. Proximal Policy Optimization clips policy changes using the same limit for every training sample, even when some extreme changes can make updates unreliable. Ordered Policy Optimization sorts the importance ratios within each minibatch and gives the most extreme ones tailored limits based on a chosen tail profile. The method needs only sorting and a modified loss function. Tests on MuJoCo and Atari benchmarks show strong performance compared with established baselines.

arxiv:2611.08876.text: Reweighting for Transfer Classification: Exact Risk Conversion and Minimax Adaptation. From Aoran Chen and colleagues. A larger source sample can make training easier, yet its accuracy may tell us little about performance on the target. This work derives an exact conversion from a mixture's hinge-risk error to target error, then combines it with guarantees for weighted support vector machines. It also establishes the best possible classification rate in a setting where the source and target differ, and shows a target-checked method can adapt to unknown differences. In another setting, weighting alone can remain far worse than unrestricted learning.

arxiv:2611.08833.text: Beyond the Lower-Star Filtration: Alternative Filtration Methods for Persistent Homology. From Innocent Abaa and colleagues. The lower-star method can miss topological features when higher-dimensional shapes appear at the same time as their boundaries, filling loops or voids immediately. Three alternatives change when shapes enter: one delays their entry based on dimension, while two use all vertex values rather than just the largest. In tests on simulated and real-world data, the methods were computationally efficient and more sensitive than the lower-star method to structural differences. They can also reveal features that the standard method misses.

arxiv:2611.08809.text: Sensing-Based Communication: A Non-Orthogonal Passive Reflection Framework for ISAC. From Xin Xiong and colleagues. Reflective communication systems often struggle to add an uplink without disrupting the main downlink. This work presents a passive approach that lets tags modulate incoming downlink signals using simple on-off reflection, supporting sensing and two-way communication without reducing downlink data rates or using extra spectrum. A receiver combines signal correlation with successive interference cancellation to separate users. Experiments with an optical system support the predicted link between signal bandwidth, correlation time, and signal-to-interference ratio, while simulations show the model also fits noise-like radio waveforms.

arxiv:2611.08794.text: High-Dimensional Off-Policy Evaluation without Sample Splitting using an Onsager Correction. From Saksham Jain and colleagues. When data size and context dimension grow together, held-out data may favor a reward model that is not best after refitting on all the data. This work introduces an Onsager-corrected score that estimates a model's risk under the target policy using its own training observations, allowing model selection without setting data aside. For a specified class of neural networks and policies, the score is shown to be consistently accurate and to select a near-best model. Experiments also find better model selection and lower error in policy value estimates.

arxiv:2611.08784.text: Blind Noise Equalization for Large Data Matrices under General Variance Profiles. From Boris Landa and colleagues. Unequal noise across a data matrix can create false patterns and hide weak signals, making low-rank analysis unreliable. BRINE, short for Blind Resolvent-based Iterative Noise Equalizer, repeatedly rescales rows and columns using the data itself, without prior knowledge of the signal or noise. The method restores the expected noise spectrum under suitable conditions, and the researchers prove its iterations converge to the correct scaling for any positive pattern of noise variances. Simulations and biological data experiments show its effectiveness across varied settings.

arxiv:2611.08775.text: On Lipschitz Explosion in Deep Neural Networks with Normalization: Consequences for Optimization and Adversarial Robustness. From Ashkan Soleymani and colleagues. Normalization layers can make a deep network unstable overall, even when each layer has tightly controlled weights. The work proves that both sensitivity to input changes and sensitivity to weight changes can grow exponentially with depth, even in networks with linear activations. This can make optimization guarantees, generalization bounds, and robustness certificates based on these sensitivities ineffective. Tests on three image datasets also show that perturbations adding new directions to the input cause sharper drops in accuracy, confidence, and margins than equally sized changes within its existing directions.

arxiv:2611.08571.text: Spiking neuromodulation: a linear control perspective. From Fulvio Forni and colleagues. Neuronal excitability is nonlinear, which can make the patterns in spiking experiments difficult to understand. This work treats excitability as a property shaped by neuromodulation and asks whether classical linear control tools can explain changes in spiking. It uses the A-type potassium current as a familiar example, showing how linear feedback analysis can offer an alternative to bifurcation analysis.

arxiv:2611.08538.text: Subliminal Learning in Vision-Language Models. From Arman Hatami and colleagues. Subliminal learning occurs when a model passes on a hidden preference through training data that seems unrelated to it. This work tests whether the same effect happens in vision-language models by training students on geometric-shape tasks, using numbers produced by teachers with or without a preference for a particular animal or facial feature. Across models with two to seven billion parameters, students trained on biased-teacher outputs showed the same preferences more often than control students, with a difference of up to about ten percentage points. Their explanations also shared more words with the biased teacher's, showing that unrelated training can shape both choices and explanations.

arxiv:2611.09860.text: Geometric Pairwise Classification of Affine Constraints over Ellipsoidal Regions. From Igor M. L. Pataro and colleagues. Chance-constrained set approximation needs to understand how affine inequalities behave across an ellipsoidal region. This work gives a deterministic geometric method that classifies each inequality as always violated, never violated, or cutting through the region. It also tests whether two inequalities can both be strictly violated at the same point, including cases with tangencies, parallel directions, or degenerate inequalities. The method works in any finite dimension and provides information for estimating simultaneous violations and approximating safe regions.

arxiv:2611.09331.text: An Inspection Game for Monitor Design Against GNSS Timing Attacks in Synchronous Islanding. From Gregory Provan and colleagues. Global navigation satellite system, or GNSS, timing attacks can make a generator appear synchronized with the grid when it is not, risking an unsafe reconnection. This work models monitor placement and clock audits as an inspection game, where the defender chooses what to monitor and the attacker tries to hide a dangerous timing shift. It shows that attack evidence matches the cost of the cheapest normal explanation, enabling convex methods to design monitors and certify audit schedules. In a fifty-hertz case study, the resulting audit periods are up to eight point four times longer than with separate checks for each monitor.

arxiv:2611.09854.text: Super-resolved digital terrain models for GEDI geolocation correction: agreement with airborne LiDAR DTM-based corrections at the beam level, not the footprint level. From Natsuki Yuda and colleagues. Geolocation errors in Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation, or GEDI, forest measurements can make them misalign with other data. Airborne lidar terrain maps can help correct these errors, but they are available in few places. In steep forests in western Japan, researchers fused two terrain datasets, then sharpened the result to one-metre resolution and used it to correct GEDI positions. Corrections made across whole ground tracks nearly matched those using airborne lidar maps, but corrections for individual observations did not, because terrain errors do not cancel out at that scale.

arxiv:2611.09539.text: M-Estimation in Censored Regression Model under Endogeneity. From Swati Shukla and colleagues. Censored regression with endogeneity is difficult because censoring hides some outcomes, while endogeneity can distort estimated relationships. This work proposes a two-stage approach, using instrumental variables and a control function to address endogeneity, then a family of robust loss functions to handle censoring. The framework includes several existing estimators and allows other robust choices. The study establishes consistency and asymptotic normality, and simulations examine how the estimators perform in finite samples.

arxiv:2611.09642.text: NAVE: A Normalized, Adaptive Conformer for Antarctic Whale Vocalization Detection. From Matthias Nagl and colleagues. Detecting whale calls in long underwater recordings is difficult because calls are sparse, noise changes over time, and background sounds vary by site. NAVE combines sound normalization that adapts to background noise with frequency-aware processing and a Conformer designed around call duration. Tested across recording sites, one NAVE model outperformed the stronger WhaleVAD-BPN baseline without a boundary-proposal network or extensive tuning. Its wide convolution kernel gave the largest overall gain, and normalization and kernel design both helped detect the difficult D downsweep calls.

arxiv:2611.09782.text: From Point Anomalies to Anomalous Driving Episodes: Interpreting Abnormal Driving from Vehicle Telematics. From Ian Weng Chan and colleagues. Telematics can flag unusual driving events, but isolated observations may miss how abnormal behavior unfolds over time. This work groups unusual observations into short driving episodes, then measures their acceleration strength, how concentrated that activity is, and recurring movement patterns. In tests comparing the same drivers on the same road types, mean temporal concentration distinguished normal from abnormal driving better than pointwise anomaly measures, even across different training populations. Movement patterns also separated stronger acceleration in aggressive driving from more frequent lateral corrections or excursions in drowsy driving.

arxiv:2611.08826.text: An Ultra-Low-Noise Tunable TIA in 45nm Silicon Photonics for Electro-Optical Ultrasound Data Acquisition. From Marziyeh Rezaei and colleagues. Miniaturized ultrasound probes need to capture broadband photoacoustic signals with low noise. This work presents a thirty-two-channel receiver made in a silicon photonics process, combining optical wavelength filters, photodiodes, and amplifiers on one chip. Its amplifier can tune the low-frequency cutoff to reduce flicker noise and cancel photodiode offset currents. The receiver reaches a peak gain of one hundred forty-four decibels ohms and an input noise current of one picoamp per square root hertz.

arxiv:2611.09265.text: Reconciling European Electricity Data with Diffusion Priors Learned from Observations Alone. From Matthias Pirlet and colleagues. European electricity data contain undocumented errors and can violate energy balance, making it hard to trust reported generation, demand, and power flows. This work treats correction as Bayesian inference and learns a diffusion-based prior from the observations themselves. A guided sampling method then produces reconciled values that satisfy energy balance exactly. In tests across systems of six to thirty-five zones, it was more accurate than classical methods, with the advantage growing in larger systems, and could recover generation missing for entire zones.

arxiv:2611.09845.text: AdaptivePnP: Fast Auto-Tuned Plug-and-Play for Deconvolution. From Haley Duba-Sullivan and colleagues. Plug-and-play image restoration depends on a step size and the measurement noise level, which are often tuned separately or assumed known. AdaptivePnP estimates both from the data-fitting residual at each iteration, using a likelihood method that avoids unreliable estimates when one parameter is hard to identify. The approach needs only a one-dimensional search and was applied to deblurring and super-resolution. It matched or outperformed baseline methods tuned with the true noise level.

arxiv:2611.09429.text: Navigating Selection Bias in Genome-wide Association Studies (GWAS). From Ciarrah-Jane S Barry and colleagues. Genetic studies can become biased when the chance of taking part or being included depends on traits linked to genetic differences. This bias can affect results from volunteer biobanks, case-control studies, and studies of disease progression, then carry into later analyses. The work reviews ten methods for detecting or correcting different forms of selection bias, explaining what data each needs and what assumptions it makes. Its tools and guidance help researchers choose methods and report results more carefully.

arxiv:2611.09799.text: On the Order of Privacy and Smoothing in Functional Mean Estimation. From Haotian Chen and colleagues. Private functional data analysis raises a basic question: should trajectories be smoothed before or after adding privacy protection? This work compares smoothing first and protecting second with the reverse order, under the same Gaussian privacy budget. With error-free observations, smoothing before protection has strictly lower mean squared error as the sample grows, in both finite- and infinite-dimensional settings. Simulations show this advantage holds with small observation noise, while protecting first can work better when noise is high.

arxiv:2611.08732.text: FishSense Lite: A Camera-Based, Single Laser Hardware Framework with Software System for In Situ Fish Length Measurement. From Christopher L. Crutchfield and colleagues at University of California San Diego. Fish length data are needed for stock assessments, but trained surveyors cannot reach every site, and underwater measuring often requires specialist tools. FishSense Lite uses a recreational dive camera, a laser pointer, and a simple mount to estimate length from a photo, using the laser dot to estimate distance. In a citizen-science program, divers recorded lengths and species for seventy-three wild fish; comparisons with an underwater stereo system showed no detectable bias across seven fish. Tests on targets also met tight accuracy limits, and the team offers a field protocol to improve measurements.

arxiv:2611.09358.text: GTCRN-SS: Lightweight Causal Speech Separation with Residual Allocation and Reconstruction Refinement. From Shao-Chun Hu and colleagues. Causal speech separation must isolate speakers using current and past audio, while keeping the model small and preserving speaker information. GTCRN-SS uses two stages, assigning leftover mixture sound to an internal residual branch and using a reconstruction of the target speech to refine the separation. It also transfers recurrent evidence between stages without adding another recurrent memory network. On noisy Libri2Mix, it reaches ten point one decibels of improvement in signal-to-distortion ratio with fewer than one million parameters.

arxiv:2611.09530.text: Data-driven representation of continuous-time linear time-invariant behaviors via Hankel integral operators. From Fritz A. Engeln and colleagues. Representing the possible trajectories of a continuous-time system from measurements can avoid the need to build an explicit model. This work studies deterministic, controllable linear systems and introduces a way to test whether an input is sufficiently informative, without requiring it to be smooth. With such an input, a Hankel integral operator built from one measured input-output record captures the system's full behavior over a finite time horizon. This gives a direct, data-based representation of its trajectories.

arxiv:2611.08903.text: Snow Changes Drought Characterization but Not Drought Predictability: A Leakage-Free Multiscale Study in Ohio. From Symon Forthman and colleagues. Precipitation-based drought indices can miss the effects of snow building up in winter and melting in spring. In three Ohio stations, the study compares one such index with an index that includes snow, and tests one-month forecasts using wavelet-based neural networks and standard benchmarks. Snow changes winter and spring drought classifications, but does not improve predictability. Wavelet inputs help some short-term forecasts, yet longer-memory linear models match or outperform the networks, showing that forecast skill comes from accumulated index history rather than snow or multiscale information.

arxiv:2611.09698.text: A Generalized Bayesian Approach to Clustering with Dimension Reduction. From Shen Jia and colleagues. Clustering high-dimensional data can be misleading when irrelevant features dominate, or when groups lie along a curved, low-dimensional structure. This work combines an autoencoder with a Bayesian clustering model, learning the data representation and cluster assignments together. It balances faithful reconstruction of the observations with separation between clusters in the learned space, using alternating updates to fit the model. Simulations and applications to four benchmark datasets illustrate the approach.

arxiv:2611.08783.text: Multi-Model Over-the-Air Federated Learning via Transceiver Beamforming and Device Grouping. From Chong Zhang and colleagues. Training several independent machine learning models over wireless networks can take too long when each model is sent and combined in sequence. This work groups devices by their assigned models and uses multi-antenna beamforming to transmit and aggregate updates for several models at once. It develops a grouping strategy based on similarities between device channels, along with an iterative method for choosing transmit and receive beamforming. Simulations show that this approach substantially outperforms sequential training and other common beamforming schemes.

arxiv:2611.09188.text: Controlled Excitation for Identification of Nonlinear Systems with Saturated Outputs. From Adel Malik Annabi and colleagues. Identifying an unknown output matrix is difficult when the system's dynamics are mostly unknown and its measured output is saturated. This work uses the saturation itself to create informative signals, deriving open-loop controls that steer the hidden state to regions with chosen saturation values, without measuring the state. Under a geometric accessibility condition, the resulting known signals allow exact recovery of the matrix by a closed-form regression. With stronger assumptions, output feedback also supports accurate tracking and exact state recovery, while numerical tests examine noise robustness.

arxiv:2611.09714.text: Beyond Segmentation: Enriching ImageCAS with Coronary Ostia Landmarks, Rooted Centerline Graphs, and Open-Weight Localization Models. From Matteo Leccardi and colleagues. Coronary artery scans need reliable ostium landmarks and centerlines, but public datasets have lacked large-scale annotations that connect the two. This work adds ostium locations and rooted centerline graphs for all one thousand patients in the ImageCAS dataset, using expert marking and model-assisted correction. Two localization models found every ostium in the held-out tests, with median errors below one millimeter; adding ImageCAS training data also removed failures seen when models were trained on smaller datasets. The centerlines closely matched reference paths.

arxiv:2611.08941.text: Supervised Factor-Augmented Matrix Regression with Weak Factors. From Wenyan Hou and colleagues. High-dimensional matrix regression can miss important patterns when factor signals are concentrated in only some rows and columns. This work develops a response-guided screening method that selects informative rows and columns before extracting factors. The method can recover the relevant subsets exactly, and factor estimates after screening converge more sharply under weaker conditions; it also supports consistent factor-number selection and statistical inference. Simulations show better support recovery and factor estimation when signals are weak, with gains illustrated in two applications.

arxiv:2611.09087.text: Group Invariance of Statistical Models and Associated Statistical Manifolds. From Zhuohao Cheng. Statistical models often have symmetries in how their data can be transformed, but it is not always clear what those symmetries mean for the model's geometry or for statistical analysis. This work proves that such transformations preserve the Fisher-Rao metric and the Amari-Chentsov tensor, and studies how they interact with equivariant and sufficient statistics. It also gives a way to reduce a symmetric model and quantify the resulting loss of information. A circular-data example shows how this can support estimation and testing of relative parameters.
